Consider the standard matrices of three linear transformations shown below. Which of the transformations map ${R}^{2}$ onto a line?

$$
{T}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}],\,{T}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{T}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 9 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a linear transformation over ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T,$ we have the following:

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto ${R}^{2}$ if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=2,$ i.e., $T$ is nonsingular.

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=1.$

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto $(0,0)$ if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=0,$ i.e., $T$ is the zero matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- ${T}_{1}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line. Notice that the columns of ${T}_{1}$ are linearly dependent but it's not the zero matrix. So, $\text{rank}({T}_{1})=1.$

- ${T}_{2}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto $(0,0)$ since ${T}_{2}$ is the zero matrix, i.e. $\text{rank}({T}_{2})=0.$

- ${T}_{3}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto ${R}^{2}.$ Indeed, ${T}_{3}$ is a nonsingular matrix, i.e. $\text{rank}({T}_{3})=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ only."

questions.problem:
Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ to the origin. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\text{rank}(T)=1$,  where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$

II. $\text{Im}(T)$ contains no vectors of ${R}^{2}$

III. $\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is the zero-subspace $\{0\},$ then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=0
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. In our case, we have 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=0.
$$

- Statement II is false. The image of $T$ contains the vector zero vector $0=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the standard matrix $T$ of the linear transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/bfab47037972e5cbb408473b3c94463b8100d622971ed66ba5dabc9ff15be7bb.svg)
Find the equation of the line that the transformation $\mathbf{T}$ maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $T$ has proportional rows, yet $T$ is not the zero matrix. 

Therefore, $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})=1$ and $\mathbf{T}$ maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto a line that passes through the origin.

Moreover, the line must pass through the origin $(0,0)$ and the points $(6,2)$ and $(-9,-3),$ which are defined by the columns of $T.$ 

Computing the slope $m$ of this line, we get

$$
m = \dfrac{-3-2}{-9-6} = \dfrac13.
$$

 

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=\dfrac13x.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying True Statements Regarding Linear Transformations in the Cartesian Plane
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ that maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=-5x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\langle -1, 5 \rangle \in \text{Im}(\mathbf{T})$

II. $\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T})=\{0\}$

III. $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})=\Bbb R^2$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\textrm{rank}(T) = \textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T}) = 1,
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the point $(-1,5)$ satisfies the equation of the line $y=-5x$ since $5=-5\cdot (-1).$ Hence, 

$$
\langle -1, 5 \rangle \in \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}).
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $\textrm{nullity}(T)=1,$ we get 

$$
\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}) \neq \{\mathbf0\}.
$$

- Statement III is false.  Since $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})=1,$ we get 

$$
\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) \neq \Bbb R^2.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have the following linear transformation: 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2
$$

The image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Therefore, it can only be one of the following:  

- the whole of $\mathbb{R}^2,$

- a line through the origin, or

- a single point (vector), namely the origin $(0,0).$

Let's denote the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ by $T.$ It turns out that the dimension of the image of $\mathbf{T}$ depends on $\text{rank}(T)$ (or equivalently on $\text{nullity}(T)$ by the rank-nullity theorem). Indeed, we have the following:

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=2,$ then the two columns of $T$ are linearly independent. This means $T$ is invertible and therefore, $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) =  \mathbb{R}^2.$

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto  $\mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/7de193042587cb9362641cbb541477a5e4951e96d9e82f074fb0cc3a86a80d3a.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/88baa47cae14d4a43d59b366c13b3c29376678edef2fe34ff505a942ef6af986.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=1,$ then there is a nonzero vector that generates the image of $\mathbf{T}.$ In this case, the image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $\Bbb R^2$. So, it is a line passing through the origin.

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=2x\mathbin{:}$ 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/4952615b0c4ddf85cc6d60483f8c0587093c67734a320cde913644fe8fdafb55.svg)
Notice that the points $(2,4)$ and $(1,2),$ defined by the columns of $T,$ lie on the line $y=2x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/0322f183c16fe82515277d10cf27a93ae753f8eadf7eeb1db4d3c5e404480b09.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=0$ then,  according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that  $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$ for all $\mathbf{v}\in \Bbb R^2$. So, in this case, we have that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/4a0ce67cffc02e28edffb9efeedca2e21ffc7c0d8b72ccfa0566cb29f6679865.svg)
which maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\{(0,0)\},$ i.e., the set containing only the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/1252907a1e9767201dd326945f328f91fc493ea283b244dbfee42a7c4248d9e6.png)

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Suppose we have the following linear transformation: 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2
$$

The image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Therefore, it can only be one of the following:  

- the whole of $\mathbb{R}^2,$

- a line through the origin, or

- a single point (vector), namely the origin $(0,0).$

Let's denote the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ by $T.$ It turns out that the dimension of the image of $\mathbf{T}$ depends on $\text{rank}(T)$ (or equivalently on $\text{nullity}(T)$ by the rank-nullity theorem). Indeed, we have the following:

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=2,$ then the two columns of $T$ are linearly independent. This means $T$ is invertible and therefore, $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) =  \mathbb{R}^2.$

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto  $\mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/7de193042587cb9362641cbb541477a5e4951e96d9e82f074fb0cc3a86a80d3a.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/88baa47cae14d4a43d59b366c13b3c29376678edef2fe34ff505a942ef6af986.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=1,$ then there is a nonzero vector that generates the image of $\mathbf{T}.$ In this case, the image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $\Bbb R^2$. So, it is a line passing through the origin.

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=2x\mathbin{:}$ 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/4952615b0c4ddf85cc6d60483f8c0587093c67734a320cde913644fe8fdafb55.svg)
Notice that the points $(2,4)$ and $(1,2),$ defined by the columns of $T,$ lie on the line $y=2x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/0322f183c16fe82515277d10cf27a93ae753f8eadf7eeb1db4d3c5e404480b09.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=0$ then,  according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that  $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$ for all $\mathbf{v}\in \Bbb R^2$. So, in this case, we have that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/4a0ce67cffc02e28edffb9efeedca2e21ffc7c0d8b72ccfa0566cb29f6679865.svg)
which maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\{(0,0)\},$ i.e., the set containing only the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14173426/assets/1252907a1e9767201dd326945f328f91fc493ea283b244dbfee42a7c4248d9e6.png)
